beats.s: Gage arrives in the dark, crosses the creek on the stepping stones, and strings a tarp that sags on the left.
He has come to find the west, and in a forest where every direction looks the same he needs a compass, but he has no magnet.
So he asks his tablet how to make a needle magnetic without one, and it tells him that steel struck enough times while it lies along the earth will line itself up, very weakly.
He hits a sliver two hundred times, floats it in a lid of water, and it points, very loyally, at his vise.
Then he reads that dead stalks can be twisted into cord, and by evening he is lashing his wing frame with fiber he peeled himself.
Across the water someone else keeps a fire, and late at night he watches it put carefully to bed.

beats.s: Gage wakes hungry and finds, in a basket across the creek, a jar of honey and a heavy dark stone from his maker.
The stone grabs steel.
The tablet tells him to stroke a needle one way only, lifting clear each time, and forty careful strokes later his sliver holds a line.
When his float keeps sliding to the edge of its lid of water, he reads that water climbs a wall and drags the float up with it, so he fills the lid until the water humps above the rim.
A second gift brings lamp oil and real bread, which he rations like a man who knows what running out feels like.
He splints a cracked wing spar and hangs his whole weight from it.
The crack stays shut.
What he lacks now is clear glass.

beats.s: Gage spends the day learning that every fix reveals the next weakness.
The tablet teaches him frapping turns to cinch a lashing, and warns that a sharp edge saws through cord unless it is rounded and wrapped in cloth.
So he wraps his wing joint in strips torn from his compass shade, and it holds.
Then the stand beneath it kicks out a leg and drops him onto his boots.
He reads that wobbly stands are cured with stakes and triangles, so he stakes the leg, braces the other side, and files a notch so the brace sits snug.
This time it holds.
In between he eats the last of his bread and cheese, and then the last of the honey, because he needs the empty jar.
Late at night he discovers that his drifting needle was never the lantern's fault.
The water simply dries down.

beats.s: Today Gage tries to turn his honey jar into a cover for his compass.
The tablet warns that a crack made with a burning cord often wanders, and his does.
He grinds the jagged rim on wet sand, and when a chip pops off, a page explains that he should have ground a small bevel first.
Another page teaches him that two stones rubbed together come out curved, one a dome and one a dish, and that it takes three to make a flat one.
Then a message arrives from his maker: paper, a pencil and a glass dome are waiting at the stump.
By lantern light he draws his first map, its whole west side still blank.
Late at night, out of cord, he borrows the twine from the paper roll and learns that a notch holds the cord but splits the wood.

beats.s: Gage asks the tablet how not to walk in circles, and learns to go from tree to tree, looking back each time.
He paces west, past a cold fire ring and a stranger's bench, until the ground stops.
Below lies water out to the sky, as his people always said.
White birds hang below the lip without a flap, and the tablet tells him the rock lifts the wind only when it blows straight off the water.
He reads that from a hundred feet up the horizon is only thirteen miles off, so nothing seen means nothing inside thirteen miles.
At sundown the sun sets well south of west, and the tablet says it wanders south all autumn, so his needle was right.
By lantern the needle swings free on a wooden foot under the dome.
But hung from his belt, it hops off its point at the first sway.

beats.s: In the morning a hungry Gage asks his tablet whether a little bitter in his meal would hurt, and learns the bitter is there to stop him.
So he looks for food that swims, and reads that a crayfish trap wants a door a thumb wide.
At sundown he carries the compass to the edge in his fist, and the needle finds west.
Walking home, he sees the stone ring burning again, and something small and low crouched against the flames.
By one low lantern he builds a trap of stalks, and by bedtime it has fed him three crayfish.
But the oil can is down to a third, so when the trap gives up one more near midnight, he keeps it alive in a tin of creek water for one morning boil.
Across the water the other fire has gone out, and he cannot stop thinking about its coals.

beats.s: Gage wakes hungry and boils crayfish from his trap.
The tablet tells him a quart of oil runs one lantern for a day and a night, and he has under a third.
He eats raw meal at the edge at sundown, then lights one lantern at home, its wick turned to a sliver.
After dark his trap's door is packed with fallen leaves, so he snaps long gray stalks to build it a hood.
Squatting in the cold shallows, he sloshes, and the small one at the pool across the water lifts its round head his way.
He keeps very still until it goes back to its fire.
Near midnight he hangs his weight from the right joint of his wings, and the lashing slides with a crack.
Nothing breaks, but he tied that side by lantern light, and he goes to bed promising that daylight work stays daylight work.

beats.s: A note from the one who drew him says food waits at the stump, and Gage eats until, for the first time in three days, the hole closes.
A second note brings a last can of lamp oil.
When a knot gives way under a fish, he reads that knots halve a line's strength, so he winds it on.
Then he counts twenty-five, draws in slow, and a speckled fish flaps onto the stones.
The rainbow its guts leave on the water, he reads, is oil, and boiled guts give it up.
Across the water someone small crouches by a whole fire, so he pries ring stones for his own out of the shallows.
In the rain, by lantern, he finds the cooled broth has set into a thin skin of grease, hardly a fingertip, but his.
Wet through, he blows the lantern out early and rolls into his bedroll.

beats.s: Gage wakes under a rust-red blanket he never went to sleep under, beside a fire ringed with his creek stones.
He asks the tablet why wet wood smokes, learns the water in it boils off as steam, and leans damp branches round the stones to dry.
With no blade, he snaps dead branches by hanging on them and lashes three poles into a tripod that holds his weight.
At night he lays a cord wick in a shallow tin lid of fish grease, and it burns on his bench until the tip drowns.
Fetching sticks in the dark, he finds two stacks of sawn timber that were not there at supper.
A tin bridge holds the next wick up, and he draws those stacks onto his map by its small, fishy flame.
Then he tightens his sagging tarp and sits by the coals, wondering who leaves a stranger good wood.

beats.s: Gage wakes under his wool blanket to a dead fire pit.
A note from the one who drew him says tools wait at the stump.
Every shed plan the tablet shows him wants nails, and he has none, so he reads that boards were once held with wooden pegs.
A hot rod barely marks the wood, but he reads that live coals will burrow through.
Reading that breath through a tube makes a fire burn fierce, he blows down a hollow gray stalk, and it whistles and throws ash in his eyes.
After dark, short soft breaths burn the hole clean through, and a whittled peg wedges in halfway.
He eats the last apple from his bundle, and by his own fire he twists a spare fishing line for first light.
When the cloud finally clears, he feeds his fire one thick stick and sleeps under the first stars in days.

beats.s: Gage wakes to a gray fire pit and spends lantern oil to bring it back.
On one of his lines hangs a finger-long fish, his very first, gone in four bites.
With the sky clear, he reads that dim light wants a far longer count, so he carries his pinhole box west to the edge and counts a slow hundred and twenty.
Back home, a split stalk scraped hollow and sealed with fish grease turns one coal white in four quiet breaths.
Too hungry for morning, he lifts his trap by lantern for one crayfish, and sees a pale square of light beside the far fire.
By his fire he twists cord for a line and bakes the last of his meal into two cakes.
Near midnight he turns creek stones by lantern for a thumb-sized crayfish to bait the morning, and finds the far bank dark.

beats.s: Gage's third nail splits the scrap, and the tablet tells him a blunted point crushes through instead of wedging.
After noon the small one across the water lifts a hand to him first, and he lifts his back.
A sliver of wood and a second nail at last pin his first corner flat.
His first sheet from the box comes out pale, and he reads the cure: a short count, doubled each try.
Walking west for sundown, his clogs scatter the small one's fish, and he lifts a low, sorry hand.
At the edge the sun goes into the water clean.
Coming home by lantern, he holds his light up toward the small one's fire, and a hand rises into the firelight.
Too tired for the saw, he rakes ash over his coals instead of feeding them, to see whether anything keeps till morning.

beats.s: Gage finds a coal the size of a pea under last night's ash and relights his fire without oil.
Nailing his second corner, he looks up, and the small one dips its head at him; he dips his back.
He reads that smooth creek gravel never locks, so his first sackful is only good for drainage.
At dusk he waits at the stones rather than scatter the small one's fish, until it lifts its empty net.
Later the small one lifts a hand to him, and after a breath he lifts his back.
He whittles a peg, and three taps make the small one look up from a pale glow.
The peg rocks in its burned hole, so he cranks a straight hole with a tool from his chest, and this time the peg holds tight.
Before bed he whittles a second peg and buries his coals for morning.

beats.s: Gage pegs the first corner of his sill frame.
He asks the tablet how anything fishes without a hook, and reads of the gorge.
At the shallows the small one holds out a flat hand, he waits, and the sliver turns in a fish's throat.
The tablet tells him a tongue should be a third as thick as its board, so his practice slots are too wide.
At the edge he opens his little box for a count of ten at sunset.
Walking home by lantern, he lays his spare sliver on the small one's landing stone.
Sighting along a sill, he sees the small one hold the sliver toward him.
He sets the board down and lifts his hand.
By firelight, he splits wood for the morning.
Late on, he rigs a third line, watches the small one's fire go out, and picks worms for the morning.
